pos: n. (Johannes Cloppenburg, 1592–1652, professor of theology at Franeker)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, Latinized Johannes; Cloppenburg, from a Westphalian place-name.
biblical_def: Johannes Cloppenburg taught at Franeker in Friesland and did two things that outlasted him. He set out the Reformed doctrine of the covenants in a form his students could use, distinguishing the covenant of works made with Adam from the covenant of grace in Christ and tracing the one covenant of grace through its successive administrations; and he wrote at length against the Socinians, who denied the deity of Christ and with it the satisfaction. Johannes Cocceius was his pupil, and the great Dutch covenant theology of the next generation grew in the ground Cloppenburg had broken. The doctrine itself is not a scheme imposed on Scripture. It is the shape Scripture takes when the promise to Abraham and the new covenant of Jeremiah are read as one work of God (Gen 17:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines covenant as a mutual consent or agreement, and administration as the management of public affairs, a dispensation.
webster_full: COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; a stipulation.
ADMINISTRA'TION, n. The executive part of government; also, dispensation; distribution; exhibition.
DISPENSA'TION, n. Distribution; the dealing out of anything; the dealing of God with his creatures.
SATISFAC'TION, n. That which satisfies; amends; atonement; payment.
scriptures: Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Gal 3:17
And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect.
Heb 8:6
But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises.
corruption_summary: Cocceius's teacher, who set the two covenants in a form a student could use.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the charge that federal theology is a seventeenth-century grid laid over the Bible. The answer is to read the texts the covenant theologians were reading. Paul argues from a covenant confirmed four hundred and thirty years before the law and insists the later could not annul the earlier; Jeremiah announces a new covenant in terms that presuppose an old; Hebrews calls the second better and the first obsolete. The structure is in the text before any theologian draws it.

The principle to recover is that God binds himself by promise and keeps the promise across generations. “And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant” (Gen 17:7). The later administration does not cancel the earlier promise: “the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul” (Gal 3:17). And the new is better by its Mediator: “he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises” (Heb 8:6).

pos: n. (Johannes Hoornbeeck, 1617–1666, professor of theology at Utrecht and Leiden)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Dutch Hoornbeeck, from a place-name meaning horn-brook.
biblical_def: Johannes Hoornbeeck wrote a survey of the religious controversies of his age, running through Jews, Muslims, pagans, Romanists, Socinians, Anabaptists and the rest, each described from its own sources and then answered; and he wrote one of the first Reformed books on the conversion of the heathen, arguing that the Dutch churches had an obligation to the peoples their ships had reached. That second book matters. The common complaint that Reformed orthodoxy had no missionary impulse is answered by its existence, and by the Dutch work in Formosa and Ceylon that lay behind it. He taught at Utrecht and then at Leiden and died at forty-nine. The commission he was arguing from is not a proposal: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations (Mat 28:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mission as a sending, a commission, and heathen as a pagan, one who worships idols.
webster_full: MIS'SION, n. A sending or being sent, usually by authority, to perform some service; persons sent; a station of missionaries.
HEA'THEN, n. A pagan; a Gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
CONVER'SION, n. A change of heart or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued.
CONTRO'VERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
corruption_summary: A survey of every religion of his age, and one of the first Reformed books on missions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the familiar claim that Reformed orthodoxy, holding election, had no reason to send anyone anywhere. Hoornbeeck held election and wrote a book urging the churches to go, which is the ordinary Reformed answer: God saves his elect by means, and preaching is the means he appointed. The decree is not a reason to sit down; it is the only guarantee that going will not be wasted.

The principle to recover is that the commission is universal in its address and the command to repent is published to all men without exception. “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19). The scope is stated again without a limit: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). And the Father's grant to the Son fixes the outcome: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance” (Psa 2:8).

pos: n. (Andreas Essenius, 1618–1677, professor of theology at Utrecht)
etymology: Greek Andreas, manly; Latinized Essenius from the Dutch surname Essen.
biblical_def: Andreas Essenius taught theology at Utrecht beside Gisbertus Voetius and shared his whole position: strict in the doctrine of the covenants, strict on the Lord's Day, opposed to the Cartesian philosophy and to the Cocceian handling of the Old Testament. His systematic theology was used in Dutch classrooms, and he wrote against the Socinians, against Rome, and against the Remonstrants. He is one of the men the word scholastic was invented to describe, and in his case it means what it ought to mean: an orderly, patient, textual exposition of the faith a church has confessed. The Lord's Day question he fought over is not trivial. The fourth commandment stands in the Decalogue and the command is to remember (Exo 20:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sabbath as a day of rest and worship, and scholastic as pertaining to the schools, in the manner of the schoolmen.
webster_full: SAB'BATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest; the day appointed for religious services, the Lord's day.
SCHOLAS'TIC, a. Pertaining to a scholar, to a school or to schools; as scholastic manners or pride; scholastic learning.
SYS'TEM, n. An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a whole plan or scheme.
REMEM'BER, v.t. To have in the mind an idea which had been in the mind before, and which recurs without effort.
scriptures: Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:
Heb 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Voetius's colleague at Utrecht: the covenants, the Lord's Day, and no quarter to Descartes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of the Lord's Day as a private preference, which the Dutch quarrel Essenius fought anticipates exactly. The Cocceian party held that the fourth commandment was ceremonial and had passed with the other shadows; the Voetian party held that it is moral, rooted in creation, and binding in the Christian Sabbath. The dictionary stands with the Voetians and with the confessions that followed them.

The principle to recover is that the day is God's, not the worshipper's, and that its keeping is described as a delight and not a deprivation. “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8). Isaiah gives the whole discipline in one clause and then names the reward: “call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable” (Isa 58:13). And the sabbath points past itself: “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).

“call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable” (Isa 58:13) — not a deprivation.
“There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9) — the day points past itself.

pos: n. (Franciscus Burmannus, 1628–1679, professor of theology at Utrecht)
etymology: Latin Franciscus, a Frank, a free man; Dutch Burman, a townsman, a burgher.
biblical_def: Franciscus Burman held the Utrecht chair as the leading Cocceian in a faculty that had been Voetian, and his systematic theology arranges the whole of divinity by the successive economies of the covenant: the covenant of works, its breach, and the unfolding administrations of grace from the promise in Eden to the consummation. The method has real strengths. It reads the Bible forward, as a history with a direction, and it keeps redemption from becoming a timeless scheme. It also has a besetting danger, which the Cocceians did not always avoid: a typology so inventive that every detail of the Old Testament becomes a prediction of some episode of church history. The discipline is in the Lord's own exposition on the Emmaus road, which was about himself and not about anything else (Luk 24:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines economy as the regular operations of nature in the generation and preservation of things, a system of management, and type as a figure or representation of something to come.
webster_full: ECON'OMY, n. The management, regulation and government of a family or the concerns of a household; a system of rules or management.
TYPE, n. A sign; a symbol; a figure of something to come; the emblem of something future.
SE'RIES, n. A continued succession of things in the same order, and bearing the same relation to each other.
EXPOUND', v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
Heb 8:13
In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
corruption_summary: The Cocceian covenant history, with a typology that needed a bridle.
corruption_paragraphs: The danger in this method is named rather than excused. When every episode of the Old Testament is read as a coded prophecy of a later century, the reader is no longer being taught by the text but by the ingenuity of his teacher, and Cocceian exposition at its worst turned the prophets into an almanac of European church history. The remedy is not to abandon typology, which Scripture plainly uses, but to take the measure from Scripture's own examples.

The principle to recover is that the Old Testament testifies of Christ, and that this is the controlling reference. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39). The Emmaus exposition names its one subject: “he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). And Paul states the second, derived use: “Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition” (1Co 10:11).

“they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39) — covenant history read forward.

pos: n. (Abraham Heidanus, 1597–1678, professor of theology at Leiden)
etymology: Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude; Latinized Heidanus from the Dutch surname van der Heyden.
biblical_def: Abraham Heidanus taught at Leiden for thirty years and was dismissed from his chair at the age of seventy-eight for defending the Cartesian philosophy after the States of Holland had forbidden its teaching in theology. He was not a heretic and the dictionary will not call him one: he held the Reformed faith, preached it, and wrote a body of divinity to teach it. What he would not concede was that the magistrate could settle a philosophical question by decree, and in that he had a point which his opponents, who had invoked the civil power, did not answer. His own position was still the mistaken one. A method that begins with universal doubt cannot be kept in a side room; it was already reshaping how his colleagues read Genesis (Pro 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deprive as to divest of an office, and conscience as the moral faculty, the internal judge.
webster_full: DEPRIVE', v.t. To divest of an office or dignity; to depose; to divest of dignity by deposition.
CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
DOUBT, n. A fluctuation of mind respecting truth or propriety, arising from defect of knowledge or evidence.
ED'ICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order, command or ordinance.
scriptures: Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Deprived of his Leiden chair at seventy-eight, and wrong on the point he would not give up.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet in this case and the dictionary names both. Heidanus was wrong to defend a method that makes the human mind the first certainty and revelation a later arrival; the order of knowing in Scripture runs the other way, from God who speaks to the creature who hears. His opponents were wrong to settle the matter by asking the States of Holland to legislate philosophy, which is the Erastian reflex and has never produced a sound conviction in anybody.

The principle to recover is that the understanding is a creature and the natural man's incapacity is not cured by method. “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5). Paul states the limit as a matter of faculty: “the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him” (1Co 2:14). And the test is external to the thinker: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

Hebrew shaan (H8172) — to lean, to support oneself upon; Proverbs 3:5.

Greek anakrino (G350) — to discern, to examine, to judge; 1 Corinthians 2:14.

“the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God” (1Co 2:14) — no method cures that.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — a test outside the thinker.

pos: n. (Christoph Wittich, 1625–1687, Cartesian theologian at Duisburg, Nijmegen and Leiden)
etymology: Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; German Wittich, from a Germanic personal name.
biblical_def: Christoph Wittich was the most able of the Cartesian theologians in the Dutch universities, and the dictionary names his central proposal and rejects it. Where the Scriptures describe the sun rising, the earth standing fast, or the heavens as a tent, Wittich held that the Holy Ghost was accommodating himself to the common speech and mistaken notions of the vulgar, so that such statements carry no truth about the natural world at all. The motive was to shield Scripture from the new astronomy. The cost was a principle with no boundary: once a class of statements is exempted from truth-telling because the audience would not have understood better, there is nothing to stop the exemption spreading. Our Lord treats the smallest mark of the text as unbreakable (Mat 5:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines accommodation as adjustment or adaptation, and tittle as a small particle, a minute part, a jot.
webster_full: ACCOMMODA'TION, n. Fitness; adaptation; adjustment of differences; reconciliation.
TIT'TLE, n. A small particle; a minute part; a jot; an iota.
VUL'GAR, a. Pertaining to the common unlettered people; plebeian; common.
INFALLIBIL'ITY, n. The quality of being incapable of error or mistake; entire exemption from liability to error.
scriptures: Mat 5:18
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: He exempted Scripture's language about nature from truth-telling, to protect it.
corruption_paragraphs: The error is named by its proper name: accommodation, in the strong sense that makes some of Scripture's statements untrue but harmless. Wittich proposed it to defend the Bible from the astronomers; the result is a Bible that speaks truly only where its readers already agree. Nineteenth-century liberalism applied exactly this principle to the miracles, to the creation account, and at length to the resurrection, and it was able to do so because the exemption Wittich introduced carried no limit within itself. The dictionary distinguishes this from the ordinary and legitimate observation that Scripture speaks in human language and from the standpoint of the observer, which it certainly does.

The principle to recover is that the whole text is true, down to its smallest mark, and that nothing in it is exempt. “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). Our Lord argues from an incidental word of a psalm and adds that “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). The purity is total: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6).

pos: n. (Melchior Leydekker, 1642–1721, professor of theology at Utrecht)
etymology: Hebrew Malki-or, king of light, through Latin Melchior; Dutch Leydekker, a slater, a roofer.
biblical_def: Melchior Leydekker held the Utrecht chair for forty years and was the last great defender of the strict Voetian position against everything that had come in with the new century. He wrote on the truth of the Reformed religion, on the covenant of grace in its Old Testament administration, and against the Cartesians, the Cocceians, the Socinians and the deists in turn. The dictionary records him because the office of a watchman is honourable even when the tide is running the other way, and his was. Within a generation of his death the Dutch churches had largely gone where he said they would go. A man in that position is not entitled to measure himself by results. He is told to keep what was committed to him (1Ti 6:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines watchman as one set to watch, a sentinel, and declension as a falling off, a decay.
webster_full: WATCH'MAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one who is set to watch, to give notice of danger.
DECLEN'SION, n. A falling off; decay; gradual failure or diminution of strength.
DE'ISM, n. The doctrine or creed of a deist; the belief or system of religious opinions of those who acknowledge the existence of one God, but deny revelation.
VIN'DICATE, v.t. To defend; to justify; to support or maintain as true or correct, against denial or censure.
scriptures: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
corruption_summary: Forty years holding the Voetian line, and the tide went the other way.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of faithfulness with success, which would make Leydekker a failure and Jeremiah a greater one. The Dutch churches of 1750 were not the churches of 1650, and nothing Leydekker wrote prevented the change. That is a fact about the eighteenth century and not a verdict on him.

The principle to recover is that the servant's charge is a deposit and his account is of keeping, not of outcomes. “O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust” (1Ti 6:20). Paul's own summary at the end names three things and none of them is a result: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). And the boundary he defended was not his to move: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28).

pos: n. (Campegius Vitringa the Elder, 1659–1722, professor at Franeker and expositor of Isaiah)
etymology: Latinized Campegius from the Frisian given name Kempo; Vitringa, a Frisian family name.
biblical_def: Campegius Vitringa spent his life at Franeker in Friesland and produced the commentary on Isaiah that was the standard Reformed exposition of that prophet for a century and a half. It is a very large book, built on the Hebrew, careful with the history, and relentless in reading the prophet's promises as fulfilled in Christ and in the gospel church. He also wrote on the synagogue, on typology, and on the Revelation. Vitringa is the answer to anyone who imagines that the high orthodox period produced only systems: here is a man who gave decades to one prophet, line by line. What he was doing, our Lord did on the Emmaus road and in the synagogue at Nazareth: the prophets testify of him (Joh 5:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prophecy as a foretelling, and exposition as a laying open the sense or meaning of a writing.
webster_full: PROPH'ECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author, or of any writing.
COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; a book of explanations or expositions.
SYN'AGOGUE, n. A congregation or assembly of Jews, met for the purpose of worship; the house appropriated to that worship.
scriptures: Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
corruption_summary: Decades on one prophet, line by line, and the standard Isaiah for a century and a half.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the historical-critical dismemberment of Isaiah into two or three authors separated by centuries, which the dictionary rejects: there is one prophet Isaiah, and the latter chapters are his. Vitringa read the book whole and read it as prophecy, which is why his exposition still has force and the nineteenth-century partition theories have mostly been abandoned even by their own successors.

The principle to recover is that prophecy is the Lord's word about his own Son and endures past every commentator. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39). The permanence belongs to the word and not to the expositor: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). And no interpreter owns it: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20).

pos: n. (Johannes a Marck, 1656–1731, professor of theology at Leiden)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Dutch a Marck, of the Mark, a territorial name.
biblical_def: Johannes a Marck wrote the textbook. His compendium of Christian theology, didactic and polemical in the same volumes, and the abridgement of it known as the Marrow, were the standard classroom divinity of the Dutch Reformed churches for more than a century, carried to the Cape and to the East by the ministers trained on them. He taught at Franeker, Groningen and finally Leiden for thirty years. A textbook is an unglamorous monument and a real one: thousands of ministers learned the order of doctrine and the texts that establish each article from his pages, and preached accordingly in villages he never saw. Paul's chain has a link for exactly this: men who shall be able to teach others also (2Ti 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compendium as a brief compilation or composition, and marrow as the essence or best part.
webster_full: COMPEN'DIUM, n. A brief compilation or composition, containing the principal heads or general principles of a larger work.
MAR'ROW, n. A soft oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones; hence, the essence; the best part.
DIDAC'TIC, a. Preceptive; containing doctrines, precepts, principles or rules; intended to instruct.
TEXT'BOOK, n. A book containing the leading principles or most important points of a science or branch of learning.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
corruption_summary: The standard Dutch classroom divinity for a century, carried to the Cape and the East.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the disdain for the handbook, as though a summary were a substitute for the Bible rather than a map of it. Marck's compendium does not replace Scripture; nearly every paragraph exists to marshal texts. A minister who has it by heart has the order of doctrine and the proof of each article, which is precisely what a man needs when he is alone in a village with a question he has never met.

The principle to recover is that teaching is a transmission with a form, and the form is given to be held. “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). The transmission is deliberate and generational: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). And the thing handed over does the building: “the word of his grace, which is able to build you up” (Act 20:32).

pos: n. (Guiljelmus Saldenus, 1627–1694, Dutch pastor and devotional writer)
etymology: Latinized Guiljelmus from Dutch Willem, resolute protector; Saldenus, a Latinized Dutch surname.
biblical_def: Guiljelmus Saldenus was a Dutch minister who served several congregations and wrote the kind of book the seventeenth-century Dutch church produced in quantity and the modern church has largely forgotten: practical treatises on the duty of self-examination, on dying well, on the reading of Scripture, on the right use of the Lord's Supper. He was trained in the strictest Utrecht divinity and used it entirely for the conscience. This is the characteristic Dutch combination at its best, scholastic precision in the study and the plainest pastoral address in the pulpit, and the two are not in competition. A man who has taken care to know what the covenant of grace actually is has something to say to a dying parishioner. The Bereans are praised for exactly this habit of personal verification (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines devotion as a yielding of the heart and affections to God, and self-examination as an inquiry into one's own state and conduct.
webster_full: DEVO'TION, n. A yielding of the heart and affections to God, with reverence, faith and piety, in religious duties.
SELF-EXAMINA'TION, n. An examination or inquiry into one's own state, conduct and motives.
PRAC'TICAL, a. Pertaining to practice or action; that may be used or applied in practice.
CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
corruption_summary: Utrecht's strictest divinity, spent entirely on the conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that doctrinal precision and warm practical religion belong to different kinds of men. The Dutch of this era disprove it in volume. Saldenus had the whole apparatus of the schools and wrote for people preparing to die, which is the test case: nothing vague is of the least use at a deathbed.

The principle to recover is that the word is to dwell in a believer and be examined by him, not merely heard. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). The Bereans are commended for verifying: “they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And the promise of intimacy is attached to fear, not to cleverness: “The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him” (Psa 25:14).
